terms.gloss: the monsoon wind of the Indian Ocean
evidence: Plin. NH 6.100: favōniō, quem hippalum ibi vocant
Plin. NH 6.104: inde ventō hippalō nāvigant
terms.comment: Pliny’s name for the west wind of the Indian Ocean, on which ships sailed from Arabia to India in midsummer: the south-west monsoon. Lewis & Short writes it with a capital, as another name of Favōnius; Pliny’s text has it as a common noun. Morgan–Owens also cites a modern coinage from the local word, ventus monsonius (Egger). For the rains it brings, see “rainy season”.

terms.gloss: the seasonal winds of the Mediterranean summer
evidence: Plin. NH 6.102: quī cursus etēsiīs flantibus peragitur XII diēbus
terms.comment: The northerly winds that blow every year in the dog days: the Mediterranean’s own seasonal wind. A comparison, not a name for the monsoon.

phrases.latin: inde ventō hippalō nāvigant diēbus XL ad prīmum emporium Indiae
phrases.english: from there they sail with the monsoon in forty days to the first trading port of India

phrases.latin: nāvigāre incipiunt aestāte mediā ante canis ortum
phrases.english: they begin to sail in midsummer, before the Dog Star rises

phrases.latin: Hippalus jam flat; mox imbrēs venient.
phrases.english: The monsoon is blowing now; the rains will come soon.

sources: Lewis & Short: Hippalus · Lewis & Short: etesiae
